note: Built incrementally from each case's verified extract; powers the merged Table of Authorities. Keyed by Indian Kanoon doc-id; each authority lists the cases that cited it and how it was treated.

15267.name: M.P. Electricity Board v. Harsh Wood Products

cited_by.proposition: No notice/opportunity required before disconnecting supply on a prima facie finding of theft; not violative of Articles 14 or 20(1) or natural justice.

755547.name: M.U. Sinai v. Union of India

cited_by.proposition: A removal-of-difficulties power may only round off angularities and cannot alter a statute's basic structure or essential provisions (para 47).

335276.name: Maharana Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. Income Tax Tribunal, Ahmedabad

cited_by.proposition: The Government's subjective satisfaction that a difficulty has arisen is not conclusive and remains open to judicial scrutiny.

1057604.name: Agricultural Market Committee v. Shalimar Chemical Works Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: The Legislature must enunciate policy and principles before delegating subsidiary legislative power.
The seven principles governing express or implied ouster of civil-court jurisdiction under a special statute.

156242701.name: Mafatlal Industries Ltd. v. Union of India

cited_by.proposition: Narrowed Dhulabhai's Principle (1): only non-compliance with fundamental statutory provisions or fundamental judicial procedure defeats the finality of a special tribunal's order.

1155660.name: Unique Butyle Tube Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P. Financial Corporation

cited_by.proposition: The principles of casus omissus and reading a statute as a whole to avoid an absurd or anomalous result.

22637242.name: M/s. Paliwal Alloys (Pvt) Limited v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd

cited_by.proposition: Held that theft of electricity under Section 135 is also unauthorised use of electricity for which assessment under Section 126 is contemplated. The sixth proviso to Section 135(1A) refers to ‘assessed amount’, confirming concurrent assessment. Right of appeal under Section 127 is available even in theft cases. Applied as controlling precedent of this Court.

181377341.name: M/s Radha Krishna Cold Storage v. State of U.P. and Others

cited_by.proposition: A Division Bench observed that mere non-mention or incorrect mention of relevant provisions does not vitiate the assessment order; the order is referable to Section 126 and appeal lies under Section 127 even where the order purports to be under Section 135.

The order under challenge is an assessment order (which can be passed only under Section 126) even if wrongly cited under Section 135; mere non-mention or incorrect mention of the relevant provision does not vitiate it. Substantive statutory rights of appeal cannot be taken away by any provision framed in subordinate rules.

897981.name: Ashok Kumar and Others v. State of U.P. and Others

cited_by.proposition: Held that unauthorised use as defined in Explanation (b) of Section 126 covers acts/omissions that constitute an offence under Section 135. The assessing officer must record its conclusion and give an opportunity of hearing before concluding that a person is indulging in unauthorised use.

Unauthorised use of electricity as defined in explanation (b) of Section 126 covers acts that constitute offences under Section 135. No person can be indicted and held guilty of unauthorised use unless given an opportunity of hearing before conclusion of assessment. Natural justice and procedural fairness require opportunity of hearing even in theft cases.

759180.name: Chairman, West Bengal State Electricity Board and Others v. Syed Mukbul Hossain and Others

cited_by.proposition: Apex Court noticed the right of appeal under Section 127 even in a case of theft of electricity, confirming that assessment procedures apply in theft cases.
Affirmed the right of appeal under Section 127 in cases of theft of electricity, confirming that assessment procedures must afford statutory appeal rights and due process.

864296.name: Tinsukhia Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam & Others

cited_by.proposition: Held that the provision of a statute must be construed as to make it effective and operative; courts should lean against any construction which tends to reduce a statute to futility. Applied to interpret Sections 126 and 135 in a harmonious manner so both are workable.

46574637.name: Varun Kumar Yadav v. State of U.P. and Others

cited_by.proposition: Held that the 24-hour requirement for lodging FIR under Section 135(1-A), Electricity Act, 2003, is not merely directory but is mandatory and imperative. Applied the principle that ‘once a particular thing is directed to be done in a particular manner, anything done otherwise will be void and illegal.’ Against this judgment, a Special Leave Petition was filed before the Apex Court (SLP (Crl.) Diary No. 74474 of 2025), with notices issued on 23.1.2026.

102224597.name: Indresh Patel @ Indreshwar Singh v. State of U.P. and 4 Others
102224597.cite: Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 265 of 2023, dated 6.2.2013

cited_by.proposition: Held that Section 135(1-A)'s 24-hour requirement is only directory, carrying no consequences for breach. Distinguished and found to be per incuriam because it failed to consider Section 57 of the Electricity Act and Clause 8.2 of the UP Electricity Supply Code 2005, both of which prescribe substantive consequences for non-compliance with the timeline.

19775419.name: Dr. Arun Kumar v. Nagar Nigam, Bareilly

cited_by.proposition: Established the foundational principle that ‘once a particular thing is directed to be done in a particular manner, anything done otherwise will be void and illegal.’ Applied to establish that the 24-hour requirement is substantive and compliance therewith is mandatory.

1652054.name: Malwa Industries Ltd. Vs. Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission

cited_by.proposition: Held that captive-user ownership may be aggregated and need not be 26% per individual member; equity shares with voting rights constitute “ownership”; and supply from a CGP to a shareholder-sister concern, without a license, is permissible subject to open-access regulations. Applied to establish that M/s. Kherani Paper Mills Ltd., holding 37.86% in the CGP owner, is a captive user.

1726045.name: Nalwa Steel & Power Ltd. Vs. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Board & Ors.

cited_by.proposition: Held that open-access regulations apply only when open access (grid) is availed of; if no grid access is used and a dedicated line serves a captive user or nearby consumer, the generating company cannot be forced to route power through the grid; and dedicated lines connecting a CGP to a load centre (including a single consumer) are permissible without a license. Relied on to support the Tribunal’s discussion of transmission rights and the distinction between dedicated-line supply and open-access supply.
